reviewer.name: Claude Sonnet, fresh subagent (cold reader 2)
reviewer.origin: Claude Agent tool subagent, model sonnet, a fresh context with only this brief and its files, launched 2026-10-26 by session_01Mxpoi6tFT3FgKmBvtGjRtS (the writer's session)

evidence: I read CONTEXT whole (section "Why doing it myself worked better for me"; the draft is the last sentence of the paragraph that begins "When I do it on my own, I can detect when the wording..."), then DRAFT, SOURCE and the_change, and formed my verdict before opening ADMISSION.json. The draft is one sentence, "I can tell when my body is saying no, before my conscious mind can twist it around to a yes." It appears once in CONTEXT, in place of "And I can notice my body saying no before my conscious mind talks me into a yes." It does what the_change says: Emulate's sentence, the body's no noticed before the conscious mind turns it into a yes. (The_change glosses it as "twist it into a yes"; the draft's own words are "twist it around to a yes", and those are what I judged.) MEANING: his published line is "I can catch the body's no before the conscious mind writes a persuasive little essay called yes." Both halves are here: catching the body's no ("tell when my body is saying no"), and doing it before the conscious mind rationalizes it into a yes ("before my conscious mind can twist it around to a yes"). "Twist" carries the spin or rationalizing sense of his "persuasive little essay", and "it" is the body's no, named at the start of the same sentence (C02 clear). One nuance I weighed: his line has the mind persuading him, the draft has it reworking the no itself. I count that as the same point, not a change of claim. Nothing is added: no new fact, no new first-person claim (C03, C04 absent). The timing ("before ... can") also lines up with the next paragraph's "quickly enough". FIT: the register is the paragraph's plain spoken one, with a casual comma before "before" and a colloquial "twist it around"; I felt no seam, and without the old "And" it still reads as the third thing he can do. The one thing a careful reader might notice is "I can tell" coming straight after "I can tell whether" in the sentence before (the replaced line said "notice"). It is plain parallel phrasing in a list of what he can do, not a distinctive phrase, so I do not count it as T26. TELL ROWS: none PRESENT. T20, T29 and T17: it is the paragraph's last sentence, but it adds a third, new ability rather than restating (without it the paragraph would end on the image ability), it states what he can do rather than handing over a compressed principle, and the replaced line already closed the paragraph on the same no/yes turn, so the change adds no landing. T02, T09 and T13: the paragraph is three "I can" sentences, but it was before the change, and the sentences carry detail (the or-list of what an image might be telling him, talking to the subconscious about the wording); the draft adds no new slot. T12: no and yes are the content, not a made symmetry. T06: the body's no is the article's own idea and is in his guide. T07, T16, T18, T19, T24, T25, T27, T28 and the C rows are clear. LINTER: "D9 follows the source order" is accepted. It is a one-sentence change whose order (catch the no, before the yes) is fixed by the sense, inside a paragraph that is otherwise unchanged, so T13 and T09 do not apply beyond what I checked above. Bookkeeping, not a fail: the ledger's T14 and T15 lines say the sentence "puts back the author's own point that Emulate dropped" and "puts back the author's words or meaning"; here nothing was put back (it is Emulate's sentence as it came), so that is template text. My own reading finds both rows absent for the reasons above.
